newsitem.title: INDIA: India-Pakistan talks go on amid political crisis.
newsitem.headline: India-Pakistan talks go on amid political crisis.

text.p: Indian and Pakistani diplomats held a third day of talks on Sunday as a political crisis threatened the future of the government in New Delhi and fresh violence flared in the disputed region of Kashmir.
India's Congress party triggered the crisis by withdrawing support from Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's ruling minority coalition and staking its own claim to form a government.
But rival Indian politicians agreed their domestic rumpus would have no impact on the fledgling dialogue with Pakistan.
"Talks are continuing between the government of India and the government of Pakistan," Foreign Minister Inder Gujral told reporters outside the prime minister's residence.
"The government of India is firmly in the saddle and the talks are continuing," declared Gujral, widely seen as the main architect of the attempted rapprochement with Pakistan.
Ghulam Nabi Azad, general secretary of the Congress Party, told Reuters discussions with Pakistan would be unaffected.
"The talks will not be affected by today's development," he said. "All the major national and international issues will be respected and treated according to the national interest."
It was not immediately clear if the Congress decision would lead to new elections or an immediate change of government.
Either way, the political upheaval appeared to add another complication to the fragile dialogue between India and Pakistan, long at odds over the Himalayan region of Kashmir.
Officials said Pakistan's foreign secretary Shamshad Ahmad and his Indian counterpart Salman Haidar met in New Delhi in the morning and afternoon, but there was no word on the outcome.
Both sides have pledged to say nothing in public until the talks, which may last until Monday, are over.
Sunday's meetings went ahead despite renewed violence in the Indian state of Jammu and Kashmir during the weekend.

Police said a grenade attack wounded four civilians in the state's summer capital Srinagar on Sunday. Nine policemen were wounded at Kupwara police station near the Pakistani border when a device tied to the body of a slain Moslem militant exploded.
On Saturday, a car bomb blast in the state's winter capital Jammu killed 16 people and wounded about 70. Farooq Abdullah, the chief minister of Jammu and Kashmir, blamed Pakistan.
"This dastardly act was sponsored by Pakistan's ISI (Inter-Services Intelligence) and its agents with the intention of dividing the people on communal lines," he said.
"The ISI doesn't want normalisation of relations between India and Pakistan and is...trying to create trouble in a bid to divide communities to further its ends," his statement added.
Jammu is populated mainly by Hindus, while Moslems form a majority in the whole state.
No one has claimed responsibility for the bombing and there has been no comment from Pakistan on Abdullah's allegation.
The India-Pakistan talks have revived a dialogue that collapsed in January 1994 over Kashmir.
Pakistan, which advocates a plebiscite in Kashmir to let its people choose whether to join India or Pakistan, wants "some progress" on the dispute before other issues can be tackled.

India says its sovereignty over Kashmir is not negotiable and has proposed putting the decades-old quarrel on the back burner. It would like agreements on promoting trade and economic cooperation and other confidence-building measures.
